procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment dated 21 November, 1968 of the Madras High Court dismissing the appeals filed by the appellant against the order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate dated 30 November, 1965 and the order of the Sessions Judge dated 16 November, 1965 acquitting the respondents.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State preferred an appeal to the High Court of Madras after the Sub-Divisional Magistrate acquitted the accused in Criminal Appeal No. 194 of 1969. The High Court held that the prosecution must fail as it was barred by limitation. In Criminal Appeal No. 195 of 1969, the State preferred an appeal to the High Court after the Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence and acquitted the respondents. The High Court maintained the judgment of the Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment of the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution of the respondents was barred by the limitation prescribed under Section 40(2) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944.

facts: The respondents were prosecuted by the State for violations of the Central Excise Rules.
In both cases, the criminal complaints were filed more than six months after the date of the alleged offenses.
The High Court had previously ruled that the prosecutions were barred by the six-month limitation period set out in Section 40(2) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944.

The State (the appellant) argued that this limitation period should only apply to legal proceedings initiated against government officers, not to prosecutions initiated by the State against private individuals.
law: Section 40(2) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, provides that no suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding shall be instituted for anything done under the Act after the expiration of six months from the accrual of the cause of action.
Section 40(1) of the same Act specifically bars suits against the Central Government or its officers.
application: The Court analyzed the language of Section 40 by comparing its two sub-sections.
It observed that sub-section (1) explicitly limits its application to suits against the Central Government or its officers.

In contrast, the Court found that sub-section (2) contains no such qualifying words. It broadly refers to "suits, prosecutions or other legal proceedings" without specifying against whom they must be instituted.

The Court reasoned that the absence of limiting language in sub-section (2) was intentional. It noted that when other statutes intend to limit such a bar to government servants only, they do so with clear and specific words.

Therefore, the Court concluded that the words in Section 40(2) are of "wide amplitude" and apply generally to any prosecution under the Act, including the one brought by the State against the respondents.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the prosecution of the respondents was barred by the six-month limitation period in Section 40(2) of the Act. The Court determined that this limitation applies to all prosecutions under the Act, not just those against government officers. Since the complaints were filed after the six-month period had expired, the Court upheld the High Court's decision to acquit the respondents.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution of the respondents was barred by the limitation prescribed under Section 40(2) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944.
appellant_arguments: The limitation provision in Section 40(2) applies only to departmental officers or Government servants, not to individuals committing offenses against the Act.
The phrase 'anything done or ordered to be done under this Act' does not cover acts that are in violation of the Act's provisions.
The protection under the section is for actions done inadvertently or mistakenly, not for deliberate and malicious acts.
respondent_arguments: The phrase 'anything done or ordered to be done' under Section 40(2) extends to illegal omissions and infractions of the statute's requirements.
The limitation period in the section applies to the prosecution of the respondents for violating the Act and its Rules.
The prosecution was rightly dismissed as it was initiated after the six-month limitation period had expired.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The phrase 'anything done or ordered to be done' under a statute includes illegal omissions and non-compliance with the statute's requirements. A statutory provision that does not contain any words of restriction or limitation regarding a class of persons is applicable to any individual or person.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the limitation period prescribed in Section 40(2) of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944, applies to the prosecution of the respondents. The court reasoned that the language of sub-section (2) is of wide amplitude, containing no qualifying words that would restrict its application only to government officers, unlike sub-section (1) or other comparable statutes. Furthermore, the phrase 'anything done or ordered to be done under this Act' was interpreted to include illegal omissions and infractions, such as the respondents' evasion of excise duty, which constitutes a failure to perform acts required by the statute. As the prosecution was initiated after the six-month period, it was correctly held to be barred by limitation.
legal_tests_applied: Comparative statutory interpretation: The court compared the language of Section 40(2) with Section 40(1) and other statutes to determine legislative intent, noting that when the legislature intends to limit protection to government officers, it does so with explicit language, which is absent in Section 40(2).

Definition of 'Omission': Citing 'Amalgameted Electricity Co. v. Municipal Committee, Ajmer', the court applied the test that a statutory 'omission' must have a 'positive content' and amount to an illegality. The court found that the non-discharge of the duty to pay excise tax met this test.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that Section 40(2) applies only to Government servants was rejected because the sub-section provides a bar of limitation 'without any qualifying words as to persons against whom suit proceeding and prosecution shall be instituted,' unlike sub-section (1) and other statutes which explicitly name Government officers.

The contention that 'anything done or ordered to be done under this Act' excludes violations of the Act was dismissed. The court held that illegal omissions, such as the evasion of payment of duty and improper use of banderols, are considered 'acts to be done or ordered to be done under the Act.'

The argument that the section does not protect deliberate or malicious acts was found to be irrelevant to sub-section (2). The court pointed out that the 'test of good faith' is an aspect of Section 40(1), but 'Sub-section (2) of section 40 does not introduce the test of good faith in relation to act done.'
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondents' argument that the phrase 'anything done or ordered to be done' under Section 40(2) extends to illegal omissions and infractions of the statute's requirements.
The court agreed that the words in Section 40(2) are of 'wide amplitude' and apply to the prosecution commenced against the respondents, not just to government officers.

The respondents' actions, such as evading payment of duty and using torn banderols, were classified as illegal omissions concerning acts required to be done under the Act, thus falling within the scope of Section 40(2)'s limitation period.
